cards.statement: By default, `helm install` applies new CRDs from `crds/` before creating an operator chart's custom resources.
cards.explanation: Helm registers definitions from crds/ before submitting chart resources that use those newly defined kinds.

cards.statement: During a chart upgrade, Helm automatically upgrades the operator's CRDs stored in its `crds/` directory.
cards.explanation: Helm leaves existing `crds/` definitions untouched during upgrades; an administrator manages their changes separately.
cards.misconception: Helm manages CRD updates as part of chart upgrades.
cards.volatilityNote: Helm may change its CRD lifecycle support in a future release.

cards.statement: When installing a network add-on, `kubectl kustomize` submits the overlay's resources to kube-apiserver.
cards.explanation: `kubectl kustomize` renders manifests; `kubectl apply -k` sends the overlay's resources to the cluster.
cards.misconception: Rendering a Kustomize overlay also installs its resources.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

cards.statement: For Pod network setup, the container runtime loads the installed CNI plugins on the node.
cards.explanation: The administrator configures the container runtime to load the CNI plugins used for Pod networking.

cards.statement: With a runtime exposing a legacy CRI API instead of CRI v1, the kubelet can still register the node.
cards.explanation: A runtime needs CRI v1 support for kubelet node registration; an older CRI API alone is insufficient.
cards.misconception: A legacy CRI implementation suffices for node registration.

cards.statement: The Kubernetes documentation recommends CNI plugins compatible with the CNI v1.0.0 specification.
cards.explanation: A plugin can support several CNI specification versions while remaining compatible with CNI v1.0.0.
cards.volatilityNote: The documentation may recommend a newer CNI specification as compatibility guidance evolves.

cards.statement: With a CSI filesystem volume in use, the driver's node plugin performs privileged mount operations on Linux.
cards.explanation: CSI node plugins perform local privileged operations needed to make storage available to Pods.

cards.statement: With differing request and storage versions, kube-apiserver saves a new custom resource in the request version.
cards.explanation: kube-apiserver stores custom resources in their CRD's designated storage version, regardless of the request version.
cards.misconception: The client's served API version selects the stored representation.

cards.statement: After creating a CRD, an administrator can check `Established` to see when its API endpoint becomes usable.
cards.explanation: A true `Established` condition signals that the custom resource endpoint is ready for requests.

source.title: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

cards.statement: Applying an operator's CRDs makes kube-controller-manager run that operator's reconciliation loop.
cards.explanation: An administrator also deploys the operator's controller, commonly as a Deployment, so its reconciliation code runs.
cards.misconception: CRD installation launches the associated operator controller.

cards.statement: A Pod using `hostNetwork: true` can reach the node's loopback listeners using `localhost`.
cards.explanation: A hostNetwork Pod shares the node's network namespace, so its loopback address reaches listeners in that host namespace.

cards.statement: An application's `localhost` listener stays isolated from other containers in the same Pod.
cards.explanation: Containers in a Pod share its IP address and port space. A loopback listener is reachable from the Pod's other containers.
cards.misconception: Containers in a Pod have separate network namespaces.

cards.statement: With node CIDR allocation enabled, the node controller manages Pod CIDR assignment for registered nodes.
cards.explanation: The node controller assigns the registered node a CIDR block when administrators enable CIDR allocation.

cards.statement: With a Pod network add-on installed, the kubelet can reach local Pods through their Pod IPs.
cards.explanation: The network model includes connectivity from node agents to Pods on that node, which lets the kubelet contact local Pods.

cards.statement: For a dual-stack Pod, an administrator gets its complete address inventory by reading `status.podIP`.
cards.explanation: status.podIP records a primary address. The assigned IPv4 and IPv6 addresses appear together in status.podIPs.
cards.misconception: The legacy podIP field contains both dual-stack addresses.

cards.statement: An administrator deploys a NetworkPolicy in the namespace containing the Pods it protects.
cards.explanation: A NetworkPolicy selects its protected Pods within its own namespace.

cards.statement: The control plane prevents edits to a namespace's `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label.
cards.explanation: The immutable kubernetes.io/metadata.name label contains the namespace's name for namespaceSelector matching.

cards.statement: An administrator can target a Service directly by name in a NetworkPolicy egress rule.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy selects traffic peers by Pod or namespace labels, or by IP ranges; Service names are outside its API.
cards.misconception: NetworkPolicy egress rules accept Service-name targets.

cards.statement: A NetworkPolicy supports client-certificate requirements for connections to selected Pods.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy controls network traffic at the IP and port level. Client-certificate checks need a TLS-aware implementation.
cards.misconception: NetworkPolicy performs TLS client authentication for Pod traffic.

cards.statement: NetworkPolicy automatically records denied connections in its standard API for an administrator to inspect.
cards.explanation: Per-connection logging is outside the NetworkPolicy API. Denial logs depend on the networking implementation.
cards.misconception: The Kubernetes API records connections denied by NetworkPolicy.

cards.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.33, the control plane tracks Service IP allocation with IPAddress and ServiceCIDR objects.
cards.explanation: IPAddress objects expose Service IP allocations to administrators through the Kubernetes API.

cards.statement: An administrator can set the cluster's initial Service IP range with kube-apiserver's `--service-cluster-ip-range`.
cards.explanation: kube-apiserver uses --service-cluster-ip-range when initializing Service address allocation.

cards.statement: For external NodePort traffic with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, kube-proxy replaces the client's source IP.
cards.explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy set to Local, kube-proxy preserves the external client's source IP for NodePort traffic.
cards.misconception: Local external traffic policy masks the client address behind a node address.

cards.statement: With `internalTrafficPolicy: Local`, kube-proxy sends ClusterIP traffic to remote endpoints if local ones are absent.
cards.explanation: For internalTrafficPolicy Local, kube-proxy drops ClusterIP traffic when the client node has no local endpoint.
cards.misconception: Local internal traffic policy falls back to remote endpoints.

cards.statement: With cloud-controller-manager, creating a LoadBalancer Service synchronously provisions the external load balancer.
cards.explanation: cloud-controller-manager provisions the load balancer asynchronously and publishes its details in the Service's .status.loadBalancer.
cards.misconception: Service creation waits for external load balancer provisioning.

cards.statement: For a Service with a selector, the control plane updates EndpointSlices as its backend Pods change.
cards.explanation: The control plane watches matching Pods and maintains the Service's EndpointSlice records.

cards.statement: `kubeadm init` configures CoreDNS by storing its Corefile in a Secret in the kube-system namespace.
cards.explanation: CoreDNS reads its Corefile from the coredns ConfigMap in kube-system. Administrators edit that ConfigMap to change server configuration.
cards.misconception: CoreDNS server configuration is stored in a Secret.

cards.statement: By default, `kubeadm init` exposes CoreDNS Pods through a Service named `kube-dns` in the kube-system namespace.
cards.explanation: The kube-dns Service name preserves compatibility for workloads across DNS implementations.

cards.statement: The kubelet configures a Pod using `dnsPolicy: Default` with resolver settings inherited from its node.
cards.explanation: dnsPolicy Default makes Pod name resolution follow the node's resolver configuration.

cards.statement: The kubelet applies `ClusterFirstWithHostNet` when a hostNetwork Pod leaves `dnsPolicy` unset.
cards.explanation: Set ClusterFirstWithHostNet explicitly for a hostNetwork Pod; leaving dnsPolicy unset selects ClusterFirst.
cards.misconception: The kubelet automatically chooses the host-network cluster DNS policy.

cards.statement: A Gateway API administrator sets a GatewayClass's controllerName to the controller's Kubernetes Deployment name.
cards.explanation: A GatewayClass's controllerName holds the implementation's assigned controller identifier. It identifies a Gateway API implementation rather than a Kubernetes Deployment object.
cards.misconception: GatewayClass controllerName refers to the Deployment object running the controller.

cards.statement: An administrator can assign different GatewayClass objects to different listeners of the same Gateway API Gateway.
cards.explanation: A Gateway names its GatewayClass through spec.gatewayClassName. Its listeners share that class and the infrastructure that implements it.
cards.misconception: A Gateway chooses a separate GatewayClass for each listener.

cards.statement: By default, a Gateway API controller considers all compatible Gateway listeners for an HTTPRoute's parentRef.
cards.explanation: A Gateway parentRef targets the Gateway's listeners by default. An administrator uses sectionName to restrict that reference to a named listener.

cards.statement: With a Gateway API controller, cross-namespace HTTPRoute attachment needs consent in the listener's allowedRoutes.
cards.explanation: A Route's parentRefs requests a Gateway attachment. The listener's allowedRoutes must also admit the Route's namespace for cross-namespace attachment.

cards.statement: A Gateway API controller accepts cross-namespace Service backends using ReferenceGrants in the HTTPRoute's namespace.
cards.explanation: The ReferenceGrant belongs in the referenced Service's namespace. The owner of that namespace grants source HTTPRoutes permission to reference its Services.
cards.misconception: The HTTPRoute's namespace contains the ReferenceGrant that authorizes its remote Service backend.

cards.statement: With a Gateway API controller, an HTTPRoute can split traffic between Service backends using relative weights.
cards.explanation: An HTTPRoute backend's share is its weight divided by the sum of the rule's backend weights. The weights express ratios rather than fixed percentages.

cards.statement: With a Gateway API controller, an HTTPRoute specifies the certificate Secret for its Gateway listener's TLS termination.
cards.explanation: A Gateway listener's TLS configuration selects the certificate Secret through certificateRefs. TLS termination configuration belongs to the Gateway.
cards.misconception: HTTPRoute selects the certificate Secret used to terminate client TLS at its parent Gateway.

cards.statement: An administrator deploys an Ingress controller as a cluster add-on to implement routing for Ingress resources.
cards.explanation: An administrator installs an Ingress controller to implement Ingress routing. Creating an Ingress resource alone does not deploy that controller.

cards.statement: With multiple Ingress controllers running, an administrator uses ingressClassName to select the handling controller.
cards.explanation: An Ingress resource's ingressClassName names an IngressClass associated with an installed controller.

source.title: Ingress Controllers — Using multiple Ingress controllers

cards.statement: Kubernetes continues adding new standard routing features to the Ingress API alongside Gateway API development.
cards.explanation: The Ingress API is frozen, so its standard feature set has stopped growing. It remains a supported, generally available Kubernetes API.
cards.misconception: Ingress remains under active API feature development alongside Gateway API.
